title: Esther Is Asked to Risk Her Life
overview: When the order to wipe out the Jews becomes public, Mordecai urges Esther to plead with the king, and after hesitating because of the deadly risk, she agrees to go.

parts.label: Mourning spreads (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Tearing clothes and wearing sackcloth, a rough cloth, with ashes were public signs of deep grief, so Mordecai was openly mourning the decree against his people. Mourning clothes were banned inside the palace gate, so he stopped just outside it, while Jews across the empire fasted and wept.

parts.label: Esther learns the news (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: Esther sent Mordecai fresh clothes, perhaps so he could come closer to the palace, but he would not accept them. Through Hathak, a palace servant assigned to her, Mordecai sent the exact sum Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury and a copy of the decree, and urged her to plead with the king.

parts.label: Esther explains the danger (vv. 9-11)
parts.note: Persian kings were kept remote, and anyone who entered the inner court uncalled could be executed unless the king held out his gold scepter, a staff that signaled he would spare them. Esther adds that the king had not sent for her in a month, which may have made her fear she had lost his favor.

parts.label: Mordecai's reply (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: Mordecai warns that the palace will not save her, since the decree covers every Jew, and that if she stays silent help will come from somewhere else. The book never names God, but many readers take this and his question about her being queen "for such a time as this" as a quiet hint that her rise was not an accident.

parts.label: Esther decides to go (vv. 15-17)
parts.note: Esther asks the Jews of Susa, the capital, to fast with her for three days, a sign of shared desperation that in Jewish practice usually went with prayer, though prayer is not mentioned. Her words "if I perish, I perish" show she knows she may die, and from here she, not Mordecai, gives the instructions.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Mordecai's talk of help arising from another place is a deliberate veiled reference to God working behind the scenes or simply his confidence that some other human rescue would come.
think: Have you ever been in a position where speaking up could cost you something real, and what made the difference in whether you did?
